tldr: We propose M3GD, a geometric diffusion model that connects independently pretrained 2D image and 3D point-cloud foundation models via camera projection, synthesizing high-quality novel view RGB and metric depth by integrating Camera and LiDAR without an additional cross-modal translator.
hero_caption: Overall view of the Camera--LiDAR multimodal representation in M3GD. Point-wise features extracted from pretrained Utonia (a 3D point-cloud foundation model) are projected into the camera frame, pooled, and arranged on the same grid as pretrained DA3 (an image geometry foundation model). This establishes natural 2D--3D correspondence without learning an extra modality translator.
overview:
When robots navigate autonomously or perform teleoperation, Novel View Synthesis (NVS)—predicting how the surroundings look from unvisited viewpoints—is critically important. While recent advances in image diffusion models enable realistic image generation, most prior methods rely solely on camera images, overlooking metric LiDAR range data that is commonly available on robotic platforms.

At the same time, camera images (dense and rich in appearance) and LiDAR point clouds (sparse, unordered, and containing precise 3D metric distances) differ fundamentally in nature. Training a massive multimodal model from scratch to combine them, or building a complex cross-modal translation network, is impractical given the high cost of collecting diverse real-robot datasets.

To address this, the authors hypothesized: "Do independently pretrained 2D image and 3D point-cloud foundation models already share a common spatial structure simply by aligning them on a 2D grid via camera projection?" Verification revealed that features from the image geometry foundation model Depth Anything 3 (DA3) and the point-cloud foundation model Utonia show strong spatial correlation through projection alone. Based on this finding, they developed M3GD. By treating the target-view LiDAR scan as an appearance-free geometric query and injecting it into an image-latent flow-matching generator via a lightweight residual adapter, M3GD achieves high-accuracy novel view synthesis without additional large-scale training.

Evaluations on the real-world GrandTour dataset demonstrate a 16% improvement in absolute relative depth error (AbsRel) over an image-only baseline, alongside enhanced visual appearance fidelity. Furthermore, zero-shot deployment on a physical robot navigating unseen outdoor environments without retraining confirms practical operation with a flexible quality--cost trade-off controlled by the number of integration steps.
contributions: Discovered and quantified for the first time that features from independently pretrained image (DA3) and point-cloud (Utonia) foundation models exhibit strong spatial and geometric alignment simply by being placed on a shared grid via camera projection.

Designed a "LiDAR packet" combining explicit geometry statistics with learned point-cloud descriptors, and proposed M3GD, a multimodal NVS method that injects it via a lightweight residual adapter without breaking the pretrained latent space or decoders.

Achieved RGB and depth synthesis accuracy surpassing the same image-only backbone on the large-scale quadruped robot dataset GrandTour, demonstrating that target-view LiDAR functions as an effective geometric query.

Demonstrated zero-shot deployment without extra training on a wheeled robot (Clearpath Warthog) with an entirely different sensor setup, verifying stable real-world operation under sensing noise and flexible inference-cost configurability.

sections.heading: Novel View Synthesis for Robotics: Why LiDAR Is Needed
sections.summary: Novel view synthesis (NVS) is essential for robot simulation and teleoperation, but conventional image-only methods struggle with textureless regions and long-range metric structure. This paper introduces M3GD, directly integrating 2D and 3D pretrained foundation models by leveraging synchronized LiDAR point clouds as appearance-free geometric queries.
sections.details:
Novel View Synthesis (NVS) is a technique for predicting what a camera would observe from unvisited viewpoints. In robotics, it is rapidly becoming an indispensable foundational technology for training and evaluating reinforcement learning policies for autonomous driving or drones inside closed-loop simulators, as well as providing blindspot-free video feeds to teleoperation operators.

However, most computer vision benchmarks focus on an "image-to-image" formulation, predicting novel RGB images exclusively from posed RGB images. In practical robot operations, cameras are frequently paired with calibrated and synchronized LiDAR sensors, making millimeter-level metric 3D structure vital. Moreover, when a mobile robot traverses an environment, a common scenario arises: "We lack an image of the target viewpoint, but we possess a LiDAR scan recorded when passing nearby." This target-view LiDAR acts as a "geometric query" that reveals the exact viewpoint position and surrounding metric geometry without leaking any unknown appearance (texture or color) to be synthesized.

The primary barrier to combining cameras and LiDAR is modality asymmetry. Images are dense, pixel-aligned, and appearance-rich, whereas LiDAR data consists of sparse, unordered 3D coordinates. Collapsing LiDAR into a single 2D depth image loses 3D structural support across layers and gaps. Conversely, training a large cross-modal translator from scratch fails to scale due to the scarce availability of well-curated multimodal robotic datasets.

This motivated the authors to ask: "Could independently pretrained 2D image and 3D point-cloud foundation models naturally share a compatible spatial structure when geometrically aligned through camera projection?" M3GD validates this hypothesis, realizing a framework that fuses both modalities using only a lightweight adapter.

sections.heading: The Intersection of Geometry-Aware Diffusion and Foundation Models
sections.summary: Prior work broadly falls into image-only generative NVS, feed-forward 3D Gaussian regression, and per-scene optimization NeRF/LiDAR integration. M3GD builds upon a geometry-latent generative diffusion backbone, bypassing test-time optimization while conditioning directly on pretrained 3D point-cloud representations.
sections.details:
To place this work in context, three major research directions should be examined.

### Generative NVS in Geometry-Aware Latent Spaces
Recent diffusion-based NVS has evolved from camera-pose-guided image generation, such as Zero-1-to-3 and CAT3D, toward making the latent space itself 3D-aware. In particular, GLD (Geometric Latent Diffusion) conducts flow matching directly on the frozen latent feature space of a geometric foundation model (e.g., DA3), decoding RGB and depth at the end with frozen decoders. Yet state-of-the-art methods like GLD remain strictly "image-only" at their inputs, lacking a mechanism to directly ingest metric data from physical 3D sensors.

### Feed-Forward Fast View Synthesis
Methods such as pixelSplat, MVSplat, and DepthSplat directly regress 3D Gaussians from sparse image inputs. While computationally fast, they lack generative priors to hallucinate unobserved appearances caused by occlusions or out-of-view regions, often introducing distortion and ghosting artifacts under wide robot baselines. Furthermore, their architectures do not accommodate LiDAR inputs.

### Depth- and LiDAR-Assisted Rendering and Foundation Model Integration
Autonomous driving simulators (e.g., UniSim, NeuRAD) and NeRF extensions (e.g., DS-NeRF, SiLVR) incorporate LiDAR as geometric regularization or loss supervision. However, these require minutes to hours of per-scene optimization for every new environment, making them unsuitable for querying novel views on the fly in real-time robot operations.

Recently, 3D point-cloud foundation models (such as Utonia) have emerged alongside language and vision models. Whereas previous methods relied on explicit distillation to align image and point features, M3GD demonstrates the Platonic Representation Hypothesis—that independently trained DA3 and Utonia naturally exhibit high spatial compatibility simply through projection—connecting them to NVS without extra cross-modal pretraining.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation and Preliminaries: Flow Matching and 2D/3D Encoders
sections.summary: We formulate the problem of predicting target-view RGB images and dense depth maps from posed source images, LiDAR, and target poses with LiDAR scans. The backbone uses flow matching with linear trajectories, alongside frozen encoders from Depth Anything 3 (DA3) for 2D images and Utonia for 3D point clouds.
sections.details:
### Problem Statement
A robot captures $N$ source views $\{(I^{\mathrm{src}}_{i},\mathsf{K}^{\mathrm{src}}_{i},T^{\mathrm{src}}_{i},P^{\mathrm{src}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$, where $I$ is an RGB image, $\mathsf{K}$ is camera intrinsics, $T$ is camera pose, and $P$ is a synchronized LiDAR point cloud. For $M$ target viewpoints $\{(\mathsf{K}^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{j},T^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{j},P^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{M}$, camera parameters and the LiDAR point cloud $P^{\mathrm{tgt}}$ are known, but RGB images $I^{\mathrm{tgt}}$ are absent. The objective is to predict dense RGB images $I^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{j}$ and full-resolution depth maps $D^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{j}$ at the target views without test-time optimization.

### Flow Matching
We employ flow matching, a continuous-time generative model, as our generator in the image-latent space. Considering a linear trajectory $z_t = (1-t)z_0 + t z_1$ between a clean latent $z_0$ and standard Gaussian noise $z_1$, the network $v_\theta(z_t, t, y)$ is trained to predict the velocity field $v = z_1 - z_0$, conditioned on $y$. At inference time, starting from noise $z_1$, the target latent representation $z_0$ is retrieved by numerically integrating the ODE backward from $t=1$ to $t=0$ using an Euler solver.

### 2D and 3D Foundation Backbones
- **DA3 (Depth Anything 3)**: A modern visual geometry foundation model predicting geometrically consistent structure from monocular or multi-view images. M3GD leverages its encoder's internal, dense image-token grid (latent space) encoding both geometry and appearance, rather than the final depth output.
- **Utonia**: A state-of-the-art point transformer self-supervised on diverse indoor and outdoor point clouds. It performs no distillation with images, yielding strong point-wise descriptors learned purely from 3D geometric structure.

sections.heading: Architecture of M3GD: Packetizing and Injecting Geometry Statistics and Point Features
sections.summary: M3GD projects and aggregates LiDAR points onto the same 2D grid as DA3, creating LiDAR packets that bundle explicit geometry statistics and learned Utonia features. Injected into the generator via a zero-initialized lightweight residual adapter, the model is efficiently trained with a target-only flow-matching loss.
sections.details:
### Overview and Latent Level Selection
M3GD builds upon the GLD pipeline operating in the image-latent space. While the DA3 encoder contains multi-scale feature maps from level 0 to 3, our representational similarity analysis revealed that Level 0 (the shallowest layer) exhibits the highest correlation with Utonia and supports direct generation. This allows M3GD to bypass GLD's original two-stage cascade (generating Level 1 before Level 0), enabling fast, single-pass inference within a single model.

### Projected RGB-LiDAR Representation (LiDAR Packets)
The LiDAR scan closest in time is transformed into the camera frame and projected onto the image plane using camera intrinsics $\mathsf{K}$. Let $\mathcal{S}_q$ denote the set of point clouds projected into each cell $q$ of the image-latent grid. For each cell, we assemble a "LiDAR packet" $\ell_q = [g_q; h_q]$ combining two components:

1. **Explicit Geometry Statistics $g_q \in \mathbb{R}^6$**:
A 6-dimensional vector comprising point presence flag $m_q$, point count $n_q$, mean depth $\bar{d}_q$, depth variance, minimum depth, and the camera-to-LiDAR capture time difference $\Delta\tau$. This directly informs the model of physical distance, sparsity, and temporal offset.
2. **Learned Point Descriptors $h_q \in \mathbb{R}^{C_u}$**:
The average-pooled frozen Utonia features of points falling inside cell $q$ ($C_u = 1224$ dimensions). Cells without points receive a zero vector.

For target views, identical LiDAR packets are constructed, acting as potent geometric queries that specify structural layout without revealing appearance.

### Residual LiDAR Conditioning (Residual Adapter)
In baseline GLD, image context tokens $c_v$ (DA3 features for source views, zero tensors for target views) are concatenated with noisy latents. M3GD extends this via a residual connection:
$$\tilde{c}_v = c_v + \phi([c_v; \ell_v; r_v])$$
where $r_v$ is a role indicator flag (source vs. target) and $\phi$ is a lightweight adapter of two $1\times 1$ convolution layers. Crucially, the final layer of $\phi$ is initialized to zero. At initialization, M3GD behaves identically to the pretrained image-only GLD, opening the LiDAR pathway progressively during training only as it helps reduce generation loss. The adapter adds approximately 1.1M parameters (about 0.2%) to the 500M-parameter transformer backbone.

### Flow Matching Training and Configurable Inference
During training, camera poses and LiDAR packets are independently dropped out with probability 0.1 to enable Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG). Since source latents are already known, we supervise the velocity MSE loss exclusively on target views $v \in \mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{tgt}}$ ("tgt-only" loss).
During inference, an Euler solver integrates the latent noise over $K$ steps. The step count $K$ can be dynamically adjusted without retraining, trading off between inference speed (fewer steps) and synthesis quality (more steps) based on robot compute availability.

sections.heading: Experimental Protocol: Datasets, Metrics, and Real-Robot Setup
sections.summary: M3GD is evaluated across 2,400 clips from diverse indoor and outdoor scenes in the GrandTour quadruped dataset. Comparisons include diffusion- and Gaussian splatting-based baselines, alongside physical deployment on a Clearpath Warthog wheeled robot.
sections.details:
### Implementation Details
Images are sized at $224 \times 336$, with a DA3 latent grid size of $H \times W = 16 \times 24$. Despite the coarse latent resolution, the model ultimately decodes full dense RGB and depth across all 75,264 pixels. Adapter $\phi$ is a two-layer Conv network parameterized as $1230 + 1536 + 1 \rightarrow 256 \rightarrow 1536$. Training runs for 50k steps using AdamW with a batch size of 32.

### Datasets and Metrics
Experiments utilize GrandTour, a large-scale multimodal dataset captured by an ANYmal-D quadruped robot. Spanning 8 challenging scenarios—ice caves, snow mountains, forests, bunkers, warehouses, and construction sites—a total of 48 logs are split into 40 training logs and 8 non-overlapping evaluation logs (2,400 clips). A challenging wide-baseline subset (1,407 clips) where camera baselines exceed 1m is also evaluated.
Evaluation covers three axes:
- **2D Appearance**: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS (perceptual distance)
- **2D Geometry (Depth)**: In the absence of ground-truth dense depth, generated RGB is passed through the DA3 encoder and DPT decoder (RGB readout) and compared against pseudo-GT to measure AbsRel (absolute relative error), RMSE, and $\delta < 1.25$ (inlier ratio)
- **3D Consistency**: 3D reprojection error and MEt3R

### Baselines
- **Diffusion Baselines**: Matrix3D, MVGenMaster, and GLD (both off-the-shelf and fine-tuned on GrandTour as GLD*†)
- **Feed-Forward Splatting Baselines**: pixelSplat, MVSplat, DepthSplat

### Physical Robot Platform
To test zero-shot transfer, we deployed M3GD onto a Clearpath Warthog wheeled UGV equipped with a MultiSense S27 stereo RGB-D camera and an Ouster 360-degree LiDAR, driven by an onboard computer with an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.

sections.heading: Results: Geometric Alignment, Baseline Comparisons, and Real-World Validation
sections.summary: Experiments confirm high alignment between DA3 and Utonia features via projection alone, with M3GD cutting depth error by 16% on GrandTour to achieve top performance. Ablations prove that LiDAR data drives these gains, and the model transfers zero-shot to an unseen wheeled robot.
sections.details:
### 2D--3D Representational Compatibility
Using ~600k image-LiDAR pairs, we evaluated the spatial alignment between independently trained 2D image features and projected Utonia features. Across linear CKA (Centered Kernel Alignment), SVCCA, and cosine neighborhood consistency (Jaccard@10), DA3 Level 0 features achieved the highest CKA and SVCCA with Utonia, outperforming other vision backbones such as DINOv2 and VGGT. PCA pseudo-color visualizations under orthogonal Procrustes alignment (Fig. F4) confirm that point-cloud and image features delineate identical objects and regions cleanly.

### Baseline Comparison
On GrandTour (Table II), M3GD secured the top score across 7 of 8 metrics.
- **Appearance (RGB)**: Yielded a modest +0.06 dB PSNR improvement over the strongest image-only baseline GLD*†, while outperforming splatting methods (e.g., +3.6 dB over PixelSplat).
- **Geometry (Depth)**: The benefits of LiDAR were pronounced. AbsRel improved by 16% ($0.173 \rightarrow 0.145$), RMSE decreased by 11% ($0.354 \rightarrow 0.314$), and the inlier ratio rose from $0.777$ to $0.810$.
- **Computational Efficiency**: Replacing GLD's two-stage cascade with single-pass inference delivered 1.7x faster runtimes and a 33% reduction in peak GPU memory usage.

### Mechanism Ablation (What Drives the Gains?)
Ablations on the challenging subset (baseline > 1m, Table VI) revealed:
- Zeroing out LiDAR packets ("Zero") or substituting fixed learnable embeddings ("Learnable param") dropped performance to match the image-only baseline (PSNR 20.37 dB). This proves that the performance boost (21.00 dB) stems directly from physical LiDAR measurements rather than added adapter capacity.
- Providing explicit geometry statistics alone ("Geom-only") captured most gains (20.90 dB), while including Utonia features provided the highest structural and texture fidelity.

### Real-Robot Deployment and Inference Trade-Offs
The model trained on GrandTour (quadruped, Hesai LiDAR) was deployed zero-shot to the Warthog UGV (wheeled, Ouster LiDAR) in a forest setting (Fig. F8). Despite occlusions, LiDAR shadows, and sensor timestamp offsets, M3GD generated consistent RGB and metric depth preserving terrain slopes and tree trunk positions.
Furthermore, varying Euler integration steps $K$ provided a controllable quality-cost trade-off. While $K=1$ ran fastest at ~3.1s (for 2 views) with degraded perceptual clarity, setting $K=5$ (~3.6s) or $K=10$ (~4.3s) sharply boosted synthesis quality to practical operating levels.

captions.F4: Feature structure visualization on the GrandTour dataset. For an RGB image, features from DA3 (image geometry), Utonia (projected LiDAR points), and DINOv2 (general vision) are reduced to 3 dimensions via PCA and colorized. Despite independent pretraining, DA3 and Utonia capture object boundaries and ground terrain with strikingly similar spatial patterns.
captions.F5: Qualitative comparison of RGB and depth synthesis on GrandTour. Feed-forward splatting methods (top) exhibit severe tearing and missing regions, while image-only diffusion models (middle) generate distorted structures due to viewpoint ambiguity. In contrast, M3GD (second from bottom) anchors generation with target-view LiDAR, recovering accurate metric geometry and appearance faithful to ground truth (bottom).
captions.F8: Real-world zero-shot evaluation on the Clearpath Warthog wheeled robot. In a forest environment, two future viewpoints (T1, T2) are synthesized from two past RGB-LiDAR observations. Despite differences in sensor configuration and temporal desynchronization, M3GD synthesizes plausible RGB images and depth maps that preserve terrain slopes and 3D tree layouts without collapsing.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work: Surface Mixing, Dynamic Objects, and Real-Time Inference
sections.summary: M3GD leaves several avenues for improvement, including depth mixing from cell-level pooling, handling dynamic objects, robustness to camera-LiDAR temporal desynchronization, and inference acceleration on edge hardware.
sections.details:
While M3GD demonstrates strong capabilities, several limitations remain toward widespread field deployment:

- **Surface Mixing from In-Cell Pooling**: Average-pooling projected point clouds within latent cells can blend foreground and background depths near object boundaries or thin wires. Incorporating visibility-aware depth weighting could mitigate this.
- **Dynamic Scenes**: The framework treats the temporally closest LiDAR scan as static geometry, causing geometric inconsistencies when fast-moving pedestrians or vehicles are present.
- **Temporal Staleness**: Although the capture time delta $\Delta\tau$ is supplied as an explicit feature, the architecture lacks continuous temporal motion compensation or uncertainty modeling.
- **Compute Requirements on Embedded Hardware**: Real-world deployment utilized a high-end desktop GPU (RTX A6000), incurring multi-second latency. Achieving true real-time rates (tens of Hz) on compact edge devices will require adaptive ODE solvers and further reduction of flow-matching steps.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Bridging 2D and 3D Foundation Models for Robotic Perception
sections.summary: Building on the discovery that independently pretrained 2D image and 3D point-cloud foundation models naturally share spatial structure via camera projection, M3GD establishes a lightweight, high-performance multimodal NVS framework. It offers a blueprint for effectively uniting foundation models in robotics.
sections.details:
M3GD harmonizes two distinct foundation models—originating from different modalities and architectures—using camera projection as a geometric bridge. By avoiding complex cross-modal translation pretraining and using a zero-initialized residual adapter, it preserves pretrained image diffusion priors while injecting metric LiDAR geometry. This provides a highly practical blueprint for robotics researchers working with constrained data and compute.

Framing target-view LiDAR as an appearance-free geometric query holds broad potential across autonomous robotics, from unvisited terrain exploration and teleoperation to closed-loop simulation for planning.

takeaways: Pretrained image (DA3) and point-cloud (Utonia) foundation models exhibit strong spatial alignment when mapped onto a shared 2D grid via camera projection, without requiring explicit cross-modal distillation.
Using target-view LiDAR as an appearance-free geometric query grounds diffusion models, preventing hallucinations and preserving accurate metric layouts under wide baseline changes.
A zero-initialized lightweight residual adapter (+0.2% parameter overhead) integrates multimodal data without degrading the capabilities of the pretrained image generative backbone.
Formulating the backbone with flow matching allows operators to dynamically adjust the Euler integration step count, tuning the latency--quality trade-off at runtime without retraining.
limitations: Average-pooling LiDAR points inside 2D latent grid cells tends to blend foreground and background surfaces near depth discontinuities and occlusions.
Static scene assumptions degrade geometric queries when dynamic objects like moving people or vehicles pass through the environment.

Deployment currently relies on workstation-grade GPUs (NVIDIA RTX A6000) with multi-second latencies, requiring further step distillation to achieve real-time rates on resource-constrained robot edge computers.
